title: Nasdaq 100 & S&P 500 Correction: What Tech Selloff Means
description: The Nasdaq 100 index experienced its most significant weekly decline since March 2020, falling by 5.6%. The S&P 500 also entered correction territory, registe.

faq.a: A market correction is typically defined as a decline of 10% or more in the price of a security, commodity, or market index from its most recent peak. It's considered a normal and healthy part of market cycles, often occurring after periods of significant gains.

faq.q: Why are AI and tech stocks particularly vulnerable during a selloff?
faq.a: AI and tech stocks are often considered growth stocks, meaning their valuations are heavily based on future earnings potential. When concerns arise about future growth, funding, or economic conditions, these stocks can experience sharper pullbacks as investors reassess their high valuations.

faq.q: How does a US market correction affect Indian investors?
faq.a: Indian investors with direct exposure to US markets through international mutual funds or ETFs will see their portfolio values impacted. Indirectly, a significant US market correction can also influence global investor sentiment, potentially leading to broader market cautiousness, including in India.

faq.q: Is this a good time to invest in tech stocks?
faq.a: Market corrections can present opportunities to invest in quality companies at lower valuations. However, timing the market is difficult. Long-term investors might consider staggered investments (SIPs) rather than a lump sum, focusing on companies with strong fundamentals.

faq.q: Should I panic sell my investments?
faq.a: Generally, panic selling is not advisable. It often leads to locking in losses and missing out on potential future rebounds. It's crucial to stick to your long-term investment plan and re-evaluate your portfolio rationally, rather than reacting emotionally to short-term volatility.

Rupee-cost averaging is an investment strategy where you invest a fixed amount of money at regular intervals, regardless of the asset's price. When prices are high, you buy fewer units, and when prices are low, you buy more units, thus averaging out your purchase cost over time.
